lead: After fourteen years Paul goes up to Jerusalem with Barnabas and Titus, and lays his gospel before the leaders, “so that the truth of the gospel might always remain with you.” In Luke, Jesus mourns over the lakeside towns that saw his mighty works and did not repent, and then gives his messengers a great dignity: “Whoever listens to you listens to me.” Both readings show the gospel carried by people who are sent, and who remain in communion with the Lord who sends them.

r.h: That the truth of the gospel might remain
set: Paul continues his account. After his first short visit to Peter (1:18), fourteen years pass. Now he goes up again, and this time the question is the one troubling the Galatians: must Gentile believers be circumcised?

Scholars discuss how this visit fits the story in Acts. Many identify it with the meeting at Jerusalem in Acts 15, where the apostles and elders decided that Gentiles were not to be burdened with circumcision; others link it with the earlier visit to bring help in a time of famine (Acts 11:29–30). Either way, Paul's point is that the leaders in Jerusalem recognized his gospel.
str: vv. 1–2: after fourteen years, with Barnabas and Titus, Paul goes up in response to a revelation and lays his gospel before the leaders.
v. 3: Titus, a Greek, is not compelled to be circumcised.
vv. 4–5: false believers try to bring them into bondage; Paul does not give way.
v. 6: the leaders add nothing to his gospel; God shows no partiality.
kw: Literally “those who are reckoned”, those of repute. In verse 9 Paul names them: James, Cephas and John.
Not a formula but the gospel's real content: that in Christ the Gentiles are received by grace through faith, without first having to become Jews.
Literally “receives a face”, a Hebrew way of speaking for judging by appearance or rank. God does not.
vv: Then after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus along with me.
Barnabas was a Jewish believer from Cyprus (Acts 4:36); Titus was a Greek. The two companions are the question in person.

Then I laid before them (though only in a private meeting with the acknowledged leaders) the gospel that I proclaim among the Gentiles, in order to make sure that I was not running, or had not run, in vain.
Paul, who received his gospel by revelation, still seeks communion with the apostles. He knows that a gospel cut off from the Church would be running in vain.
we did not submit to them even for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel might always remain with you.

The “false believers” of verse 4 were members of the Church who insisted on circumcision; Paul's quarrel is with them, not with the Jewish people. His firmness is for the sake of others: “with you”. He defends the Galatians' place in the family of God.
ch: The Church has always seen in this meeting, together with Acts 15, a pattern for settling questions of faith: the apostles meet, listen and decide together under the Holy Spirit. The Catechism teaches that the college of bishops, united with the successor of Peter, carries on this care for the whole Church (CCC 880–883). Paul's words also stand behind the Church's teaching that our justification comes from the grace of God (CCC 1996), a grace that bears fruit in “faith working through love” (Galatians 5:6).

r.h: Whoever listens to you listens to me
set: Jesus is on his way to Jerusalem and has sent out seventy messengers ahead of him (10:1). He has told them what to do when a town does not receive them (10:10–12). Now he turns to the towns beside the Sea of Galilee, where so many of his mighty works had been done.

Chorazin lay in the hills a few kilometres north of Capernaum. Bethsaida, the town of Andrew, Peter and Philip (John 1:44), lay near the place where the Jordan enters the lake. Tyre and Sidon were Gentile cities on the coast, often rebuked by the prophets (Isaiah 23; Ezekiel 26–28).
str: vv. 13–14: woe to Chorazin and Bethsaida; Tyre and Sidon would have repented.
v. 15: Capernaum will be brought down to Hades.
v. 16: whoever listens to you listens to me; whoever rejects you rejects me and the one who sent me.
kw: A cry of grief as much as of warning, the word of a lament. Jesus mourns over these towns as he warns them.
Literally “powers”, the word the first three Gospels use for the miracles. They were signs calling for a change of heart.
To change one's mind and turn one's life around. Sackcloth and ashes were the outward signs of such turning (Jonah 3:6).
vv: Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida!
Chorazin is named only here and in Matthew's parallel (Matthew 11:21), and no miracle there is recorded. We learn from this verse how much Jesus did that is not written (John 21:25).
And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? No, you will be brought down to Hades.
The words recall Isaiah 14:13–15, the taunt against the proud king of Babylon. Capernaum, the town Jesus made his home, is warned not to be proud of its privilege.
Whoever listens to you listens to me, and whoever rejects you rejects me, and whoever rejects me rejects the one who sent me.
A chain of sending, from the Father to Jesus to his messengers. The Easter Church lives by it: the risen Lord still speaks through those he sends.
ch: The Second Vatican Council quotes verse 16 when it teaches that the bishops have succeeded the apostles as shepherds of the Church, so that whoever hears them hears Christ (Lumen Gentium 20). The Catechism recalls the same words when it explains why the faithful receive the teaching of their pastors with docility (CCC 87). This is not a claim to human greatness: the messengers carry a word that is not their own.

qa: Why did Paul refuse to have Titus circumcised, when Acts says that he had Timothy circumcised (Acts 16:3)?

The two cases were different. Titus was a Greek, and some were demanding his circumcision as necessary for salvation; to give way would have denied that we are saved by the grace of Christ. Timothy had a Jewish mother, and Paul had him circumcised by his own choice, so that he could work among Jews without giving offence (Acts 16:1–3). Paul was firm on the principle and flexible in love (1 Corinthians 9:20).
study: Paul defended “the truth of the gospel” with firmness and in communion with the apostles. Where do I need both courage and communion in my faith?
Jesus says, “Whoever listens to you listens to me.” How do I listen to the pastors and teachers of the Church in my life?
